sections.content: The preterite tense is the backbone of historical narration: it presents a chain of completed, one-after-another events (departed, sighted land, landed, died) rather than an ongoing state. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Cristóbal Colón partió del puerto de Palos de la Frontera el 3 de agosto de 1492 con tres barcos.
items.english: Christopher Columbus set sail from the port of Palos de la Frontera on August 3, 1492 with three ships.

items.spanish: El 12 de octubre, un marinero de la Pinta llamado Rodrigo de Triana avistó tierra por primera vez.
items.english: On October 12, a sailor from the Pinta named Rodrigo de Triana sighted land for the first time.

items.spanish: Colón murió en 1506 sin admitir jamás que no había llegado a Asia.
items.english: Columbus died in 1506 never admitting that he hadn't reached Asia.

items.spanish: En 1507, un cartógrafo alemán llamado Martin Waldseemüller publicó un mapa que bautizó el nuevo continente.
items.english: In 1507, a German cartographer named Martin Waldseemüller published a map that named the new continent.

sections.content: Reach for the preterite (*partió, avistó, murió, publicó*) whenever a historical text moves the story forward one finished event at a time. Save the imperfect for description or background that was ongoing at the time (*la tripulación estaba nerviosa*) — most history-book sentences lean heavily preterite.
